theme: Faith from hearing; the mystery of Israel; doxology
readingInstruction: Read Romans 10:1-11:36. This is a long reading, so take it in two parts: chapter 10 on faith that comes from hearing, and chapter 11 on God’s plan for Israel and the Gentiles. End with the doxology in 11:33-36.
settingTheScene: Chapter 9 stressed God’s sovereign choice. Chapter 10 emphasizes human responsibility: Israel’s problem is that they did not submit to God’s righteousness, and the message is open to all who call. Chapter 11 asks the question that remains: has God rejected his people? Paul’s answer reveals a mystery of God’s plan across history, and it ends with one of the great praise passages in Scripture.
observation: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (10:4).
“Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (10:9).
“So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (10:17).
“I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means!” (11:1).
“So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace” (11:5).
“And in this way all Israel will be saved” (11:26).
“Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (11:33).
“For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (11:36).
interpretation:
Paul begins with prayer: “Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.” He admits they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. Being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” The word “end” can mean goal or termination. Probably both: Christ is the goal toward which the law pointed, and its termination as a way of righteousness.

The message of faith is near: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” And the heart of it: “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.” The confession is “Jesus is Lord,” the earliest creed, and it is joined with belief in the resurrection. It is for everyone: “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him. For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

Then the chain of missions: “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” This passage has sent generations of missionaries. “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.” Israel has heard but not obeyed. God has held out his hands to a disobedient and contrary people.

In chapter 11, Paul asks: has God rejected his people? “By no means! For I myself am an Israelite.” God has not rejected the people whom he foreknew. There is a remnant, chosen by grace: like the seven thousand in Elijah’s day. Others were hardened, but their stumbling has meant salvation for the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous.

Paul warns the Gentile believers with the picture of the olive tree. Branches were broken off because of unbelief, and wild olive branches (Gentiles) were grafted in. “Remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.” Do not be arrogant. And the broken-off branches can be grafted in again if they do not continue in unbelief.

Then the mystery: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved.” Christians disagree about what “all Israel” means. Some think it refers to the whole elect people of God, Jew and Gentile together. Others think it means the ethnic nation of Israel, who will turn to Christ in large numbers before or at the end. Others hold that it means the elect of Israel throughout history. All agree that God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable, that he will be faithful to his promises, and that salvation for both Jew and Gentile comes only through faith in Christ.

The long argument ends not with a conclusion but with praise. “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.” When theology reaches its limit, it turns to worship.
connection: Deuteronomy 30:11-14 is quoted in 10:6-8. Joel 2:32 is quoted in verse 13. Isaiah 52:7 is quoted in verse 15. Isaiah 53:1 is quoted in verse 16. Deuteronomy 32:21 and Isaiah 65:1-2 are quoted in 10:19-21. 1 Kings 19:10-18 is the story of the seven thousand. Jeremiah 11:16-17 and Hosea 14:6 use the olive tree. Ephesians 2:11-22 speaks of Jew and Gentile made one. Galatians 6:16 mentions the Israel of God. Isaiah 40:13 is quoted in 11:34. Job 41:11 is quoted in verse 35. Revelation 7:9-10 pictures the worshiping multitude.
application:
Memorize Romans 10:9 and share it with someone this week.

Pray for someone to be sent to those who have not heard. Consider how you can support missions.

Let the doxology in 11:33-36 be your prayer after a difficult question.
prayerPrompts: Confess Jesus as Lord with your mouth and tell him you believe God raised him.
Pray for someone to hear and believe.
Praise God for the depth of his wisdom.
